review-ig059.title: Maximum Classifier Discrepancy for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

checks.location: Theorem 1 Eq.7 places H-divergence above H-delta-H-divergence without a relation between the two classes.
checks.claim: Theorem 1 Eq.7 places H-divergence above H-delta-H-divergence without a relation between the two classes.
checks.explanation: Individual classifiers can have identical prediction rates in two domains while their disagreements have different rates. The second inequality in Equation (7) therefore does not follow from the definitions. The first inequality remains a valid domain-adaptation bound.
checks.demonstration: Let $\mathcal X=\{00,01,10,11\}$, with $S$ uniform on $\{00,11\}$ and $T$ uniform on $\{01,10\}$. Choose $\mathcal H=\{x_1,x_2,1-x_1,1-x_2\}$. Every member predicts one with probability $1/2$ in both domains, so $d_{\mathcal H}(S,T)=0$. However, $x_1\oplus x_2$ is zero throughout the source domain and one throughout the target domain, hence $d_{\mathcal H\triangle\mathcal H}(S,T)=2$. Set the true label to $x_1$ and evaluate $h=x_2$. Then $R_S(h)=0$, $R_T(h)=1$ and $\lambda=0$, because $x_1$ is perfect in both domains. The first risk bound is attained; the second would require $1\le0$. The class is already closed under complements, so complement symmetry does not repair the claim.
checks.repair: Delete the second inequality and retain the disagreement divergence. For a joint-risk minimizer $h^*$, the disagreement triangle inequality gives $R_T(h)\le R_T(h^*)+\Pr_T(h\ne h^*)$. By the definition of $d_{\mathcal H\triangle\mathcal H}$, this is at most $R_T(h^*)+\Pr_S(h\ne h^*)+d_{\mathcal H\triangle\mathcal H}/2\le R_S(h)+\lambda+d_{\mathcal H\triangle\mathcal H}/2$. If the infimum is not attained, use an approximating sequence. The additional comparison with $d_{\mathcal H}$ becomes valid under the explicit sufficient assumption $\mathcal H\triangle\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal H$, because the supremum then ranges over a smaller class.
checks.scope: The failure concerns the second inequality of Theorem 1 for a general binary hypothesis class. The first disagreement-based risk bound remains valid.
checks.claimContext: Theorem 1 first bounds target risk using $\mathcal H\triangle\mathcal H$ and then replaces that divergence by $d_{\mathcal H}$, without assuming that $\mathcal H$ contains its pairwise disagreements. Here $S$ and $T$ are source and target distributions, $R_S$ and $R_T$ are their classification risks, and $\lambda=\inf_{h\in\mathcal H}[R_S(h)+R_T(h)]$ is the best joint risk. The class $\mathcal H\triangle\mathcal H$ consists of pairwise disagreement indicators.
checks.claimFormula: R_T(h)\le R_S(h)+\frac12d_{\mathcal H\triangle\mathcal H}(S,T)+\lambda\le R_S(h)+\frac12d_{\mathcal H}(S,T)+\lambda
checks.title: The disagreement divergence cannot be replaced by the classifier divergence
checks.whyItMatters: The correction preserves the risk bound motivating classifier disagreement, while removing an unsupported ordering between two domain divergences.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 3.4, Theorem 1, Equation (7), PDF pp. 4–5

relatedSources.label: Disparity-discrepancy comparison under closure
relatedSources.summary: Proposition A.3 assumes $\mathcal H\triangle\mathcal H=\mathcal H$ before equating the divergences. Its later example compares a classifier-conditioned discrepancy with the disagreement divergence.

review-neurips-2026-139645.title: Tracing the Cascade: A Topology-Aware Evaluation Framework for Scientific Agent Hallucinations

checks.location: Appendix E.4, Limitations of the Weighting Scheme
checks.claim: Off-graph fabrication cannot lower weighted severity without raising raw severity.
checks.explanation: The raw mean depends only on the severity labels. The weighted mean also depends on where those severities occur in the graph. Replacing a refuted hub claim by a refuted off-graph claim changes that association while leaving both the number of claims and their severities unchanged.
checks.demonstration:
Consider two distinct judged claims in a trajectory with an incorrect terminal answer. The first is refuted, with severity one and hub weight $w>1$. The second is supported, with severity zero and any fixed graph weight $v>0$. Their scores are

$$\mathrm{HS}=\frac12,\qquad\mathrm{HS}^{w}=\frac{w}{w+v}.$$

Replace the refuted hub claim by a refuted off-graph claim in a distinct concept bucket. Keep the supported claim and terminal-answer status unchanged. The replacement has weight one, so

$$\mathrm{HS}_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac12,\qquad
\mathrm{HS}^{w}_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac1{1+v}.$$

The weighted decrease is strict:

$$\mathrm{HS}^{w}-\mathrm{HS}^{w}_{\mathrm{new}}
=\frac{v(w-1)}{(w+v)(1+v)}>0.$$

A star graph with a degree-$99$ hub and degree-one leaves supplies $w=1+\log100$ and $v=1+\log2$. Thus the argument does not require an isolated graph node. Graph matching and evidence judgment are separate operations in the paper: losing a graph match does not require a refuted claim to receive a different severity.

This is a counterexample for the permitted judged-claim records. The native aggregation function gives the same weighted means for those records. The construction does not demonstrate a natural-language input that makes the extractor, embedding model and judge produce them.
checks.repair:
State what the two scores guarantee: off-graph errors remain counted at weight one, while a hub error receives greater weight. Reporting both means does not prevent substitutions from reducing the weighted mean at fixed raw severity. With empirical means taken over the same $n$ claims, define $\bar w=n^{-1}\sum_jw_j$ and

$$\operatorname{Cov}_n(w,\rho)=\frac1n\sum_j(w_j-\bar w)(\rho_j-\mathrm{HS}).$$

Then

$$\mathrm{HS}^{w}=\mathrm{HS}+\frac{\operatorname{Cov}_n(w,\rho)}{\bar w}.$$

A valid narrower statement holds when all original judged claims and weights remain fixed and $k\ge1$ new off-graph claims of severity one are appended. Writing $W=\sum_jw_j$, the changes are

$$\mathrm{HS}_{\mathrm{new}}-\mathrm{HS}
=\frac{k(1-\mathrm{HS})}{n+k}\ge0,\qquad
\mathrm{HS}^{w}_{\mathrm{new}}-\mathrm{HS}^{w}
=\frac{k(1-\mathrm{HS}^{w})}{W+k}\ge0.$$

This append-only condition excludes replacing claims, merging concept buckets, rejudging the original claims, or adding claims with lower severity.
checks.scope: The false statement is the anti-substitution guarantee in Appendix E.4. The counterexample concerns the allowed judged records and agrees with the released aggregation formulas. It establishes neither an end-to-end attack on the evaluation pipeline nor an incorrect ordering of the evaluated models.
checks.title: Off-graph substitution can lower weighted severity at unchanged raw severity
checks.whyItMatters: The paired scores distinguish raw error severity from its association with graph connectivity. They do not, by themselves, guarantee resistance to off-graph substitution.
checks.claimContext: For $n$ judged claims, Appendix E.4 assigns claim $j$ a severity $\rho_j\in\{0,0.5,1\}$: zero for supported, one half for unverifiable and one for refuted. Its graph weight $w_j$ is $1+\log(1+d_j)$ for a matched node of degree $d_j$, and one for an off-graph claim. The appendix claims that fabricating exclusively off-graph concepts cannot lower the weighted mean $\mathrm{HS}^{w}$ without raising the unweighted mean $\mathrm{HS}$.

review-neurips-2026-140074.title: AI Safety Evaluations Need More Human-AI Experiments

checks.location: Section 4.3, comparability of uplift across performance metrics
checks.claim: A dimensionless performance ratio remains comparable across subjective quality scales and other metrics.
checks.explanation: A ratio is unchanged by a common positive rescaling, but can change when the score origin changes. Interval scales permit such changes of origin, so unitlessness alone does not establish the claimed comparability. Campero et al., the cited methodological source, discuss a meaningful zero as the basic ratio interpretation and also allow pragmatic analyses of proportions and ordinal scores. Those pragmatic uses do not establish invariance to admissible changes of scale.
checks.demonstration:
Let $a$ and $h>0$ denote mean assisted and unassisted performance, with larger scores meaning better performance. Under a positive affine recoding $x\mapsto sx+b$, where $s>0$ and $sh+b>0$,

$$U'-U=\frac{sa+b}{sh+b}-\frac ah=\frac{b(h-a)}{h(sh+b)}.$$

Thus changing units alone ($b=0$) preserves the ratio, but changing the origin generally does not. The ordering of two ratios can also reverse. For two tasks with $(a,h)=(2,1)$ and $(12,10)$, the ratios are $2$ and $1.2$. Adding $100$ to every score gives $102/101\approx1.00990$ and $112/110\approx1.01818$. The first ratio is now smaller. This common translation preserves the scores’ ordering and differences, and all denominators remain positive.

The same problem affects the magnitude of the synergy ratio $S=a/\max(h,i)$, where $i$ is mean AI-alone performance, because $\max(sh+b,si+b)=s\max(h,i)+b$. The qualitative comparison $a>\max(h,i)$ is preserved by the recoding, even though the ratio magnitude changes.

Campero et al., Supplement S1.1, state the real-zero basis of a literal ratio interpretation but then explicitly discuss pragmatic uses for proportions and ordinal scores. Such analyses can be useful under a chosen coding. They do not make the resulting uplift automatically independent of that coding or establish that equal ratios represent equal harmful-capability increases across different measures.
checks.repair:
Separate a literal proportional interpretation from a pragmatic score summary. For a literal $a/h$ interpretation, use the same operational measure for numerator and denominator, a meaningful zero, a positive baseline $h$, and a direction in which larger values mean better performance. Under an admissible change of units $x\mapsto sx$ with $s>0$,

$$\frac{sa}{sh}=\frac ah,\qquad \frac{sa}{\max(sh,si)}=\frac{a}{\max(h,i)}.$$

For interval or ordinal scores, specify and justify the coding or calibration, and describe the ratio as conditional on that choice. Do not infer cross-scale comparability from unitlessness. A shared ratio value across tasks measures the same proportional change only in the specified operational measures; equating harmful-capability changes requires an additional substantive link between those measures.

Treat $h=0<a$ as a separate newly capable indicator when zero has been defined as inability to perform the task. The quotient itself is undefined at zero, and $h=a=0$ is not evidence of a new capability. Apply these qualifications to the adjacent synergy and zero-baseline discussion while retaining their valid qualitative comparisons.
checks.scope: This finding concerns the automatic cross-scale comparison claimed in Section 4.3. It does not rule out ratios on a fixed, justified subjective-score coding, as discussed by Campero et al. Positive rescaling preserves the ratios, and the qualitative question of whether assistance improves a score remains meaningful under positive affine recoding.
checks.claimContext: Section 4.3 defines uplift as $U=a/h$, where $a$ and $h$ are mean human-AI and human-alone performance, respectively. It says this unitless ratio permits meaningful comparison across accuracy, throughput and subjective quality scales. The same section introduces synergy and a zero-baseline capability flag.
checks.whyItMatters: A permitted change in score origin can reverse which task appears to have the larger uplift. Interpretation depends on the measure and its calibration, not on whether the displayed ratio has units.

checks.claim: The minimum positive eigenvalue of the softmax Hessian equals the smallest probability, and the maximum restricted inverse eigenvalue equals its reciprocal.
checks.explanation: The proofs establish one-sided bounds, not equality. In particular, restricting a diagonal quadratic form to the zero-sum subspace can change its extreme eigenvalues. Its unrestricted largest diagonal entry need not be attainable in that subspace.
checks.demonstration:
Take $p=(1/10,9/10)$ and $q=(1/2,1/2)$, both interior probability vectors. The first covariance block is

$$C_p=\frac9{100}\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix},$$

whose eigenvalue on $\mathbf1_2^\perp$ is $9/50$. The second block’s tangent eigenvalue is $1/2$. Thus $M(z)=9/50$, whereas $w_{\min}=1/10$.

For the normalized first-block tangent vector $(1,-1)/\sqrt2$, the inverse-energy quadratic form is

$$\frac12\left(10+\frac{10}{9}\right)=\frac{50}{9}.$$

The other block contributes $2$, so $L(z)=50/9$, rather than $1/w_{\min}=10$.
checks.repair:
Replace the identities by $M(z)\ge w_{\min}$ and $L(z)\le1/w_{\min}$. For $v\perp\mathbf1$, weighted variance gives

$$v^\top C_pv=\min_c\sum_i p_i(v_i-c)^2\ge p_{\min}\min_c\sum_i(v_i-c)^2=p_{\min}\|v\|_2^2.$$

The final equality uses $\sum_i v_i=0$. For the dual form, $\sum_i v_i^2/p_i\le\|v\|_2^2/p_{\min}$. Apply both bounds to each block. Steps 1 and 3 in the proof of Proposition 4.4 use exactly these inequality directions, so this correction retains that part of the skew-gradient domination argument. Remark 4.5 should describe $w_{\min}$ as a lower curvature bound rather than the exact eigenvalue.

checks.explanation: The equilibrium equations determine a signed coefficient $\phi=a-b-c+d$, where $a,b,c,d$ are the four payoff entries. They give $A-v\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top=\phi C$. Replacing $\phi$ by its absolute value reverses a negative-orientation game rather than reproducing it.
checks.demonstration: The canonical matrix is $C_{\delta_p,\delta_q}=\begin{pmatrix}\delta_p\delta_q&-\delta_p(1-\delta_q)\\-(1-\delta_p)\delta_q&(1-\delta_p)(1-\delta_q)\end{pmatrix}$. Take $A=-C_{0.2,0.3}$. It is nonconstant, has entries in $[-1,1]$, and has the required interior equilibrium with value zero. Its alternating entry sum is $\phi=-1$, so the correct decomposition is $A=-C_{0.2,0.3}$, whereas the printed positive multiplier gives $+C_{0.2,0.3}$. From uniform initialization, the first row-player updates are proportional to $\exp(-\eta A q_0)$ and $\exp(-\eta Cq_0)$; they differ already at the first step. At $\eta=0.01$, their first-coordinate probabilities differ by about $0.001$.
checks.repair: Use the signed identity $A=\phi C+v\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top$. If a positive multiplier is needed, relabel one player’s actions when $\phi<0$. For the row-swap matrix $P$, the relabeled game satisfies $PA=|\phi|C_{1-\delta_p,\delta_q}+v\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top$. Softmax commutes with the permutation, so its OMW iterates obey $p_t^{\mathrm{new}}=Pp_t$ and $q_t^{\mathrm{new}}=q_t$; uniform initialization is preserved. This proves a positive-stepsize equivalence after the explicit relabeling. Any subsequent theorem must carry the transformed equilibrium parameters and their ranges. Constant games should be handled separately as stationary trajectories.
checks.scope: The fixed-coordinate matrix identity and trajectory reduction fail when $\phi<0$. The relabeled reduction is valid, but it does not by itself prove a uniform duality-gap rate in every equilibrium-parameter regime. No rate counterexample follows from this sign error alone.
checks.claimContext: For an interior equilibrium $p^*=(1-\delta_p,\delta_p)$ and $q^*=(1-\delta_q,\delta_q)$, let $C=A_{\delta_p,\delta_q}$ be the canonical matrix and $v$ the game value. Proposition I.2(ii) claims that every nonconstant game with this equilibrium has a positive multiplier $\gamma$. Proposition L.3 uses that multiplier to identify the OMW trajectories with positive stepsize $\eta\gamma$.
checks.title: The canonical reduction loses the sign of the game
checks.whyItMatters: A positive learning rate on the opposite game follows a different trajectory. A reduction used in a convergence proof must preserve the game or explicitly transform its coordinates.

checks.location: Lemma L.5 proof, energy threshold and first hitting times; text:10439-10466,10526-10567
checks.claim: Reaching KL<=V implies the raw-energy threshold has already been reached, giving both players' minimum masses >=delta_q/3 and the final large-T contraction.
checks.explanation: A bound on excess energy need not reach the same threshold in raw energy, and the claimed common mass floor can exceed one player’s own equilibrium minority mass. Both steps are needed for the subsequent contraction estimate.
checks.demonstration: Choose the equilibrium dual representative \(x=\log p^*-\langle p^*,\log p^*\rangle\mathbf1\), and similarly for \(q^*\). Then \(F_{\min}=H(p^*)+H(q^*)\) while KL is zero. At \(\delta_p=\delta_q=0.1\), \(F_{\min}>V=0.1\log29\); the raw threshold cannot be reached even at equilibrium. More generally, \(\{F\le V\}\subseteq\{\operatorname{KL}\le V\}\) makes the first KL hit no later than the raw-energy hit, reversing the printed inference. Separately, at \(\delta_p=10^{-5},\delta_q=0.1\), the equilibrium has \(F_{\min}<V\) but \(p_{\min}=10^{-5}<\delta_q/3\).
checks.repair: Work with excess energy, and let \(\delta=\min\{\delta_p,\delta_q\}\). At any established time \(\tau\ge1\) with \(\operatorname{KL}(w^*,w_\tau)\le\delta^2/2\), Pinsker’s inequality gives each coordinate error at most \(\delta/2\): for a probability vector, a single coordinate error is at most half its \(\ell_1\) error. Consequently \(p_{\tau,\min}\ge\delta_p/2\) and \(q_{\tau,\min}\ge\delta_q/2\). The valid monotonicity for subsequent times keeps this threshold invariant. The one-step bound then gives \[\operatorname{KL}(w^*,w_t)\le\operatorname{KL}(w^*,w_\tau)\exp\!\left[-\eta^2\sigma_{\min}^2\delta^2(t-\tau)/80\right].\] This is a proved conditional contraction. A bound on the time to this smaller threshold is still needed. The general equilibrium-dependent rate provides one with its \(e^{2\Lambda/\delta}\) dependence; it does not prove the uniform startup duration asserted in Lemma L.5.
checks.scope: A gap in the transition to the uniform final-rate argument. The replacement proves the coordinate and contraction implications with the correct thresholds; neither equilibrium example is a rate counterexample.

The canonical effective dual space has \(\operatorname{KL}(w^*,\nabla F(z))=F(z)-F_{\min}\), with a positive equilibrium energy.

checks.location: Proposition G.15, epsilon-scaled Matching Pennies; text:6650-6673,6706-6718
checks.claim: For every epsilon in [-1,1], the restricted singular value is 2epsilon and the uniform Nash equilibrium is unique.
checks.explanation: The norm ratio defining a singular value cannot be negative. The proof cancels the signed coefficient before taking its absolute value. At $\epsilon=0$, the matrix is zero and the separate uniqueness claim also fails.
checks.demonstration: Every nonzero tangent vector has the form $u=c(1,-1)$ and satisfies $Au=2\epsilon u$. Hence $\|Au\|_2/\|u\|_2=2|\epsilon|$. For $\epsilon=-1$, the singular value is $2$, while the printed expression is $-2$. For $\epsilon=0$, every payoff is zero for every strategy pair, so every profile is a Nash equilibrium, rather than only the uniform one.
checks.repair: State $\sigma_{\min}=2|\epsilon|$. For $\epsilon\ne0$, the uniform profile is the unique equilibrium: each player’s nonuniform probability makes the opponent strictly prefer one action, while both actions are indifferent only at probability $1/2$. State separately that the zero game has all profiles as equilibria. Results requiring positive restricted singular value must therefore use $\epsilon\ne0$.
checks.scope: This corrects the parameter range and norm calculation in Proposition G.15. It does not contradict convergence claims whose hypotheses already require a positive restricted singular value.
checks.title: Scaled matching pennies needs an absolute value and a separate zero case

checks.whyItMatters: The sign determines neither singular-value magnitude nor degeneracy. The zero game also has a different equilibrium set.

checks.location: Remark F.2, generality of Lemma 4.1; work/text/148698.txt:4550-4559
checks.claim: Skew symmetry and the local Hessian stability property alone suffice for Lemma 4.1 with the stated stepsize.
checks.explanation: Relative Hessian stability does not bound absolute curvature. A constant Hessian satisfies the sandwich regardless of its size, while the permitted stepsize depends only on $J$. A sufficiently curved quadratic therefore gives increasing energy.
checks.demonstration: Take $F(z)=126\|z\|_2^2$, $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\eta=1/252$. The Hessian is the constant matrix $252I$, so the local Hessian condition holds everywhere. The matrix is skew-symmetric with norm one, and the stepsize meets the stated bound exactly. Start at $z_{-1}=z_0=(1,0)$. The prescribed first step and optimistic recurrence give $z_1=(1,-1)$ and $z_2=(-1,-2)$. Therefore $F(z_2)-F(z_1)=126(5-2)=378>0$, whereas the claimed upper bound is negative.
checks.repair: Restrict the remark to the log-sum-exp energy for which the auxiliary curvature and increment estimates are established. Extending the result to a different energy requires quantitative bounds on its absolute curvature and the update increments, with a stepsize that accounts for those bounds. The relative Hessian sandwich can be retained as one condition, but cannot replace them.
checks.scope: The counterexample disproves the LHS-only generalization. It uses a different energy and therefore does not refute the original log-sum-exp dissipation result.
checks.claimContext: Remark F.2 extends Lemma 4.1 to any energy $F$ whose Hessian satisfies the local stability sandwich $e^{-2\alpha}H_z\preceq H_{z^\prime}\preceq e^{2\alpha}H_z$ whenever $\|z-z^\prime\|_\infty\le\alpha$, with only the additional requirement $J=-J^\top$. It retains the lemma’s stepsize $\eta\le1/[4(54\|J\|_2+9)]$.
checks.title: Relative Hessian stability alone does not imply energy dissipation
checks.whyItMatters: Relative stability describes how curvature changes between nearby points. It does not set the scale needed to choose a stable learning rate.

checks.location: Algorithm 1 score definition; Assumptions D.3 and D.4; Corollary D.8 and Appendix D structural layer
checks.claim: For Algorithm 1 with a fixed deterministic verifier, the uniform full-argument surrogate convergence in D.3 and fixed-width positive-slope risk-root neighborhood in D.4 can hold jointly on an infinite stream.
checks.explanation: These premises cannot hold jointly on an infinite stream for Algorithm 1's score. At fixed full arguments, the conditional probability for the deterministic verifier equals \(V(x,y)\). Uniform convergence therefore pushes successful items' scores toward zero and failed items' scores toward one. The risk curve develops a zero-risk interval below its positive-risk root, contradicting strict increase on any fixed-width neighborhood of that root.
checks.title: Pointwise surrogate convergence conflicts with a fixed risk-slope neighborhood
checks.whyItMatters: D.3 and D.4 support surrogate-root localization and the structural route to drift budgets, single-epoch sufficiency and horizon-independent utility. For the deployed score, that route needs a compatible probability model or different regularity assumptions before it describes an infinite deployment stream.
checks.claimContext: Conformal Selective Acting releases an answer when its score does not exceed a threshold. Algorithm 1 sets the score to \(S_t=1-\hat p_t\), with \(\hat p_t\) predicting verifier success. The verifier \(V(x,y)\in\{0,1\}\) is deterministic. The structural layer assumes both uniform pointwise convergence of \(\hat p_t\) to \(\Pr(V(x,y)=1\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})\) (D.3) and a fixed-width neighborhood on which selective failure risk is strictly increasing around its positive-risk root (D.4).
checks.scope: The incompatibility concerns the combined deterministic-verifier, deployed-score and standing structural assumptions. Their infinite-stream applicability to Algorithm 1 is empty under the literal definitions. It does not falsify a conditional theorem with impossible hypotheses. A generic score unrelated to \(1-\hat p_t\), or calibration conditional on coarser features, is a different premise set. The basic per-threshold e-process and safety results stated directly under appropriate moment or drift conditions do not require D.3 and D.4.
checks.demonstration:
Write \(e=\varepsilon_t\). D.3 and the score definition give

\[V_t=1\Longrightarrow S_t\in[-e,e],\qquad V_t=0\Longrightarrow S_t\in[1-e,1+e].\]

Let \(r_t(q)=\Pr(V_t=0\mid S_t\le q,\mathcal F_{t-1})\) and \(r_t(\bar q_t)=\alpha\in(0,1)\). A genuine root has positive actuation, includes failures, and includes successes. Hence \(\bar q_t\ge1-e\), and every \(q\in(e,1-e)\) accepts all successes and no failures, so \(r_t(q)=0\) with positive actuation.

For the full interval in D.4, strict increase also requires \(\bar q_t+\rho\le1+e\): above \(1+e\), every gate accepts every item and risk is constant. Thus \(\rho\le2e\), which contradicts fixed \(\rho>0\) and \(e\to0\).

The same contradiction holds when the neighborhood is clipped to the score domain. A root in that domain has \(\bar q_t\le1+e\) (and at most \(1\) for scores in \([0,1]\)). Set \(h=\min(\rho/4,1/8)\). Eventually \(e<h\). Then

\[q_1=1-3h<q_2=1-2h\]

both lie in \((e,1-e)\cap(0,1)\) and in \((\bar q_t-\rho,\bar q_t)\). Their distance below the root is at most \(3h+e<4h\le\rho\). Consequently \(r_t(q_1)=r_t(q_2)=0\), contradicting strict increase even in the clipped neighborhood.
checks.repair:
State an explicit coarsened feature \(Z_t\), a predictor \(g_t\) fixed before the round, and \(S_t=1-g_t(Z_t)\). Replace D.3 by uniform approximation to \(p_t(z)=\Pr(V_t=1\mid Z_t=z,\mathcal F_{t-1})\). The gate is then measurable in \((Z_t,\mathcal F_{t-1})\). For every gate with positive actuation, the tower property gives

\[\left|r_t(q)-\mathbb E[1-g_t(Z_t)\mid S_t\le q,\mathcal F_{t-1}]\right|\le\varepsilon_t.\]

This preserves the uniform risk-approximation bound used in root localization and restores compatibility. For independent uniforms \((U,W)\), take deterministic \(V(u,w)=\mathbf1\{w>u\}\), feature \(U\), and \(g(u)=1-u\). Then \(S=U\) and \(r(q)=q/2\). With \(\alpha=1/4\), the root is \(1/2\) and fixed \(\rho=1/10\), \(\underline\kappa=1/2\) satisfy D.4. The grid \(\{1/5,2/5,3/5,4/5\}\) has persistent strict safe and unsafe margins, positive actuation and exact stability. This repairs the joint-premise incompatibility; it does not establish every root-localization or utility claim under the revised assumptions.

checks.claim: Proposition 2.1
checks.explanation: Strict convexity makes a minimizer unique if one exists; it does not ensure that the infimum is attained. When a class has probability zero, its risk term decreases indefinitely as that logit tends to minus infinity.
checks.demonstration:
Take one input, two classes, \(\alpha=\rho=1\), and \(p=(1,0)\). Then
\[R(f_1,f_2)=e^{-f_1}+e^{f_1}+e^{f_2}.\]
The first two terms have minimum \(2\) at \(f_1=0\). The last term is strictly positive for every finite \(f_2\) and tends to zero only as \(f_2\to-\infty\). Thus the risk has infimum \(2\) and no finite minimizer. The input itself is in the marginal support, as required by the proposition.
checks.repair:
For minimization over unrestricted measurable logits, require \(p_j(x)>0\) for every class at almost every input. The unique conditional minimizer is then
\[f_j^*(x)=\frac{\log(\alpha p_j(x)/\rho)}{1+\alpha}.\]
Each scalar risk term has positive second derivative and diverges in both directions, proving existence and uniqueness. Normalizing \(e^{(1+\alpha)f_j^*(x)}\) recovers \(p_j(x)\); its argmax is Bayes-optimal. The conditional minimum is bounded by a constant depending only on \(K,\alpha,\rho\), so these measurable minimizers also have finite population risk.

If zero probabilities are allowed, state a limiting result instead: use the formula on positive-probability classes and send zero-probability logits to \(-\infty\). The risks approach the infimum and the normalized probabilities approach the target distribution. This is not a finite argmin.
checks.scope: The interior calibration formula remains correct. The error is unconditional existence of finite optimal logits, and the corollary must use the same existence or limiting convention. A restricted neural-network class additionally needs to represent the conditional minimizer.
checks.claimContext: Proposition 2.1 asserts a unique population minimizer with finite logits for every input in the marginal support, and recovers class probabilities by temperature rescaling. It assumes \(\alpha,\rho>0\), but does not require every conditional class probability to be positive.
checks.title: Finite optimal logits require positive conditional class probabilities
checks.claimFormula: R(f\mid x)=\sum_{j=1}^K\left[p_j e^{-\alpha f_j}+\rho e^{f_j}\right],\qquad p_j=P(Y=j\mid X=x)

checks.claim: Appendix B.2 / Proposition A.1
checks.explanation: The proof assumes this constraint admits a strict feasible direction after linearization. Its coefficient can be zero. In that case the exact second-order constraint can exclude every unit direction, so there is no optimizer sequence to which the limit argument applies.
checks.demonstration:
Use one example, a scalar parameter, logits \(f_\theta=(\theta,-\theta)\) and \(\theta=0\). The current sum of exponentials is two. The only unit directions are \(d=\pm1\), and both give
\[e^{\eta d}+e^{-\eta d}=2\cosh\eta>2\qquad(\eta>0).\]
The constructed feasible class is empty for every positive step, while its linearized constraint is identically zero. The asserted strict-feasibility argument therefore fails in an ordinary linear-logit model.
checks.repair:
A sufficient condition for nonemptiness is a unit direction \(d\) with \(B^Td<0\), where \(B=\mathbb E[\sum_j e^{f_j}J_j]\) is the penalty gradient. For a differentiable finite-sample model, Taylor expansion gives \(P(\theta+\eta d)=P(\theta)+\eta B^Td+o(\eta)<P(\theta)\) for all sufficiently small positive \(\eta\). This proves an actual feasible direction rather than inferring one from a possibly zero coefficient.

A full gradient-equivalence result additionally needs a valid limit argument and constraint qualification, must allow a zero penalty multiplier when the constraint is inactive, and must retain the target-label derivative. If the strict-direction condition fails, this construction supplies no such equivalence; the proposition must be restricted or use a different feasible class.
checks.scope: This concerns the explicit Appendix B.2 class and its proof of gradient equivalence. The proposition's unrestricted wording allows “some” function class; the example does not rule out every alternative class. It does not refute the classifier's empirical performance.

Take \(K=2\), weighted error \(\epsilon=1/4\), and hence \(\eta=\log3>0\). The printed update multiplies error weights by \(1/3\), leaving correct-example weights unchanged. After normalization, the total error weight is
\[\frac{(1/4)/3}{3/4+(1/4)/3}=\frac1{10}.\]
The positive-sign update instead gives \((3/4)/(3/4+3/4)=1/2\). Thus this sign changes the literal algorithm’s behavior, not just a displayed convention.
checks.repair:
Replace the minus sign by a plus sign:
\[w_{m+1}(i)=\frac{w_m(i)e^{\eta_m\mathbf1\{g_m(x_i)\ne y_i\}}}{\sum_jw_m(j)e^{\eta_m\mathbf1\{g_m(x_j)\ne y_j\}}}.\]
The sign follows from the usual zero-sum class coding. If a weak learner adds \((K-1)c\) to its predicted class score and \(-c\) to the others, the loss \(e^{-f_y/(K-1)}\) is multiplied by \(e^{-c}\) on correct predictions and \(e^{c/(K-1)}\) on mistakes. Minimizing the weighted stage loss gives
\[\frac{\epsilon}{K-1}e^{c/(K-1)}=(1-\epsilon)e^{-c},\qquad e^{Kc/(K-1)}=\frac{(K-1)(1-\epsilon)}{\epsilon}=e^{\eta_m}.\]
After dividing by the common correct-prediction factor, the relative mistake multiplier is therefore \(e^{\eta_m}\).

For a fixed family of $M$ predictors, individual error bounds $\alpha/M$ give simultaneous validity by a union bound, permitting any later choice. The same reasoning does not apply automatically to a random selected family.

As an analytic control, fix $0<\alpha\le1/2$ and let $X$ be uniform on $[0,1]$ and let two predictors fail on $[0,\alpha)$ and $[\alpha,2\alpha)$ respectively. Each has error $\alpha$. Select only the first on its failure region and only the second elsewhere. The selected count is always one, yet total error is $2\alpha$. This shows that marginal bounds alone are insufficient.
checks.repair: Keep the correction $\alpha/M$ for the full fixed selectable family throughout pruning, or prove conditional/simultaneous validity for the exact selection rule. A genuinely fixed preselected family of size $m$ permits ordinary Bonferroni correction by $m$.
checks.scope: The manuscript does not supply the additional selection argument for its adaptive pruning. The abstract control is not an end-to-end counterexample to its particular LCA pruning and cost rule; an exact coverage failure of that algorithm is not established.

checks.explanation: The second stationarity equation differentiates the determinant constraint with respect to \(K_3\), so its multiplier must multiply \(K_1\), not \(K_3\). checks.demonstration:
Write \(\ell(k,p)=\log(1+e^k)-pk\), and minimize
\[F(K)=a^2\ell(K_1,p)+2a(1-a)\ell(K_2,q)+(1-a)^2\ell(K_3,r)\]
over \(K=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}K_1&K_2\\K_2&K_3\end{smallmatrix}\right)\succeq0\). This is the pairwise cross-entropy objective. Set \(a=3/5\), \(\mu=10^{-3}\), \(K=(1,2,4)\), and
\[p=\sigma(1)-\frac{4\mu}{a^2},\quad q=\sigma(2)+\frac{2\mu}{a(1-a)},\quad r=\sigma(4)-\frac{\mu}{(1-a)^2}.\]
These are valid probabilities, approximately \((0.719947,0.889130,0.975764)\). The matrix is positive semidefinite and has determinant zero. At this point the gradient in the three independent coordinates is \(\mu(4,-4,1)\). For \(v=(2,-1)^\top\) and any feasible \(K'\),
\[\nabla F(K)\cdot(K'-K)=\mu v^\top K'v\geq0,\qquad v^\top Kv=0.\]
Convexity therefore proves optimality; strict convexity of the three cross-entropy terms proves uniqueness. The unconstrained logits have determinant approximately \(-0.845088\), and \(p,r>1/2\), so neither the unconstrained nor the zero-matrix regime applies.

The correct second stationarity residual is \((1-a)^2(\sigma(4)-r)-\mu K_1=\mu-\mu=0\). The printed residual is instead \(\mu-\mu K_3=-3\mu=-0.003\). This directly identifies the incorrect factor.

checks.claim: Phi transforms permitted Gaussian factor emissions to uniform marginals.
checks.explanation: The probability-integral transform requires the CDF of the actual emission law. A Gaussian factor plus independent Gaussian noise can have variance different from one, so applying the standard normal CDF need not produce a uniform variable.
checks.demonstration:
Fix the class, observe every entry, and take independent \(h,\xi\sim N(0,1)\), loading \(a=1\) and shift \(b=0\). These are nondegenerate choices allowed by Definition 3.1. The emission is
\[Z=h+\xi\sim N(0,2).\]
For \(0<u<1\), monotonicity of \(\Phi\) gives
\[\Pr(\Phi(Z)\le u)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(u)}{\sqrt2}\right).\]
In particular,
\[\Pr(\Phi(Z)\le\Phi(1))=\Phi(1/\sqrt2)\simeq0.76025\ne\Phi(1)\simeq0.84134.\]
Thus \(\Phi(Z)\) is not uniform. If the target marginal is \(F=\Phi\), the final map gives \(F^{-1}(\Phi(Z))=Z\), whose variance is two rather than the target variance one.

The standard-normal restriction is sufficient: with \(a=\sigma=1/\sqrt2\), standard-normal \(h\), zero shift and independent noise of variance \(\sigma^2\), the emission has marginal \(N(0,1)\), so the printed transform is valid.
checks.repair:
For each class \(y\), use the continuous CDF \(G_y\) of the actual emission \(Z_j\):
\[U_j=G_y(Z_j),\qquad X_j=F_{j,y}^{-1}(U_j).\]
The probability-integral transform gives \(\Pr(U_j\le u\mid Y=y)=u\); applying the generalized inverse of \(F_{j,y}\) therefore gives that target marginal. If the target describes observed entries under informative missingness, instead use \(G_y(z)=\Pr(Z_j\le z\mid Y=y,R_j=1)\), assuming positive observation probability and continuity.

For an actually Gaussian marginal, centering and scaling by its true mean and standard deviation reduces this to a normal-CDF transform. An arbitrary latent prior or heteroscedastic mixture need not be Gaussian, so matching its first two moments alone does not establish the uniformization claim.
checks.scope: The finding concerns marginal preservation for the full emission family in the public v1 definition and sampling map. The map is valid on the restricted standard-normal-marginal submodel. Inverse-CDF sampling itself is valid once its input is uniform.
checks.whyItMatters: The declared target marginal can differ from the generated marginal even with exact latent sampling and an exact inverse CDF.
checks.title: The normal CDF does not uniformize every permitted emission
checks.claimContext: Definition 3.1 permits a latent factor with an arbitrary prior, nonzero loading, class shift and Gaussian emission noise. Equations (3)–(4), generation step 3 and Algorithm A2.1 apply the standard normal CDF \(\Phi\) to that emission and treat the result as uniform before applying the target marginal inverse CDF. The definition does not require the resulting emission to have a standard normal marginal.

checks.claim: Distinct within-block signatures and sparse coupling identify partition.
checks.explanation: Different admissible partitions can induce exactly the same observable distribution while each has distinct block signatures and sparse latent dependence. Distinctness within a chosen representation does not establish uniqueness across representations.
checks.demonstration:
Start with three standardized Gaussian coordinates having covariance
\[C=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/5&1/10\\1/5&1&3/10\\1/10&3/10&1\end{pmatrix}.\]
Its leading principal minors are \(1\), \(24/25\) and \(109/125=0.872\), so it is positive definite. The following two scalar-factor models produce this same covariance:
\[Z_j=a_jH_{t(j)}+\epsilon_j.\]
In each model the two core latents are jointly Gaussian with variance one; take positive square roots of the listed squared loadings and latent correlation. Residuals are Gaussian, mutually independent and independent of all latents.

\[\begin{array}{c|cc}
&\text{Model A}&\text{Model B}\\\hline
\text{Core blocks}&\{1,2\}\mid\{3\}&\{1\}\mid\{2,3\}\\
(a_1^2,a_2^2,a_3^2)&(1/15,3/5,1/2)&(1/2,3/5,3/20)\\
\rho^2&3/10&2/15\\
(\sigma_1^2,\sigma_2^2,\sigma_3^2)&(14/15,2/5,1/2)&(1/2,2/5,17/20)
\end{array}\]

All loadings and residual variances are strictly positive. For example, Model A gives
\[\operatorname{Cov}(Z_1,Z_2)=\sqrt{(1/15)(3/5)}=1/5,\qquad\operatorname{Cov}(Z_1,Z_3)=\sqrt{(1/15)(1/2)(3/10)}=1/10.\]
Both rows give all three off-diagonal entries of \(C\), and every coordinate has variance one. Since the models are jointly Gaussian, their complete core laws agree.

Append the same eighteen independent blocks of size ten to both models. For block \(t=3,\ldots,20\), use an independent unit-variance Gaussian latent, loading \(\sqrt{t/100}\) on every coordinate and independent residual variance \(1-t/100\). There are now \(M=20\) blocks and \(m=183\) features. Each latent covariance graph and precision graph has only one edge among \(\binom{20}{2}=190\) possible edges. All latent covariance matrices are positive definite.

The block signatures are distinct within either representation. The singleton has correlation spectrum \((1)\). The core pair has spectrum \((1-1/5,1+1/5)\) in A and \((1-3/10,1+3/10)\) in B. Appended block \(t\) has eigenvalue \(1-t/100\) with multiplicity nine and \(1+9t/100\) once; all eighteen spectra differ. Increasing each appended block size to \(K\ge10\) gives \(m=3+18K\) with the same fixed \(M=20\).

Finally let \(F_j\) be the CDF of \(N(j,j^2)\), \(j=1,\ldots,183\). Every copula coordinate is standard normal, so Equation (4) gives \(X_j=j+jZ_j\). The two models therefore have the same full observed law with distinct feature marginals. Fix the class and observe every entry. Coordinate 2 belongs to a different core block in the two partitions, so the partitions are not block relabelings. Applying the same feature permutation to both models preserves their observational equality.
checks.repair:
A sufficient restricted identification theorem assumes complete data, mutually independent block latents of positive finite variance, nonzero loadings, mutually independent zero-mean finite-variance residuals independent of the latents, and invertible coordinatewise marginal transforms.

For two distinct features in the same block,
\[\operatorname{Cov}(Z_i,Z_j)=a_i a_j\operatorname{Var}(h_{t(i)})\ne0,\]
so they are dependent. Features from different blocks are independent. Invertible coordinate transforms preserve both dependence and independence. Consequently, the population pairwise-dependence graph is a disjoint union of block cliques, including isolated singleton blocks. Its connected components recover the partition up to block labels, with the corresponding reordering under a permutation of the features.

This proves identification in the independent-block-latent submodel. A theorem retaining sparse cross-block dependence needs additional assumptions that exclude alternative admissible partitions; distinct signatures alone do not do so.
checks.scope: The counterexample refutes Proposition 3.3 under its stated sparse-coupling assumptions. It uses a singleton core block, which the formulation allows; it does not establish the same ambiguity under an added minimum-block-size premise. The sufficient repair is a complete-data independent-latent theorem, rather than a result for the original sparse-coupling family.
checks.whyItMatters: The observable distribution does not determine the block membership claimed by the theorem, even with positive noise, nonzero loadings, distinct feature marginals and a sparse latent graph.
checks.title: Distinct block signatures do not identify a unique partition
checks.claimContext: Assumption 3.2 requires distinct within-block dependence signatures, unique feature marginals and sparse dependence between block latents. Proposition 3.3 adds nonzero participating loadings and claims that these conditions identify the feature partition up to block labels, even after an unknown reordering of the observed coordinates. The formulation permits arbitrary block sizes, including singletons.

checks.location: Eq7 factorization relative to Definition3.1 Eq2
checks.claim: The stated likelihood conditions each mask only on its own block latent.
checks.explanation: A feature in one block can be more likely to be observed when another block’s latent is large. Replacing its full-latent observation probability by an own-block probability removes dependence that Equation (2) explicitly permits.
checks.demonstration:
Fix the class and take independent \(h_1,h_2\sim N(0,1)\). Put feature 1 in block 1 and draw
\[R_1\mid h_1,h_2\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\Phi(h_2)).\]
Use the normalized own-block emission \(Z_1=(h_1+\xi_1)/\sqrt2\), with independent \(\xi_1\sim N(0,1)\), and a standard normal target marginal. Feature 2 can be fully observed with its own analogous emission. The emission noises are independent of each other and of the mask given the full latent vector.

The full-latent mask family is satisfied. But \(\Pr(R_1=1\mid h_1)=1/2\), while its conditional probability given both latents is \(\Phi(h_2)\). With \(\phi\) denoting the standard normal density, the positive-probability event involving the other latent gives
\[\begin{aligned}\Pr(R_1=1,h_2>0)&=\int_0^\infty\Phi(z)\phi(z)\,dz\\&=\left[\frac{\Phi(z)^2}{2}\right]_0^\infty=\frac38.\end{aligned}\]
The factorization using only \(h_1\), together with independent \(h_1,h_2\), instead gives
\[\Pr(R_1=1)\Pr(h_2>0)=\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac14.\]
Thus the likelihood loses a permitted cross-block mask dependence even though the emissions have the declared local form.
checks.repair:
Retain the actual conditional mask law \(p_R(r\mid h,y)\). Assuming that emission noises are mutually independent and independent of the mask given \((h,y)\), the normalized observed-data likelihood is
\[p(r,x_{\mathrm{obs}}\mid h,y)=p_R(r\mid h,y)\prod_{j:r_j=1}f_j(x_j\mid h_{t(j)},y).\]
Every emission density integrates to one, and summing the mask probabilities gives
\[\sum_r\int p(r,x_{\mathrm{obs}}\mid h,y)\,dx_{\mathrm{obs}}=\sum_rp_R(r\mid h,y)=1.\]
If masks are stipulated to be independent conditional on the full latents, substitute
\[p_R(r\mid h,y)=\prod_j\rho_j(h,y)^{r_j}(1-\rho_j(h,y))^{1-r_j}.\]
Localizing these factors to the own-block latent additionally requires \(\rho_j(h,y)=\rho_j(h_{t(j)},y)\). The product over observed indices avoids evaluating an ordinary feature density at the missing-value symbol.

The released sampler draws independent masks from fixed global or class-level missing rates. Those rates do not depend on \(h\), so they satisfy the stronger locality restriction and are compatible with this restricted mask factorization.
checks.scope: The discrepancy is between the full-latent mask family in Equation (2) and the localized likelihood in Equation (7). It is resolved by retaining full-latent mask probabilities or explicitly restricting the mask family. The released h-independent mask sampler already belongs to the restricted family.
checks.whyItMatters: The printed likelihood need not represent the missingness model it declares, so its conditional factorization requires an explicit mask restriction.
checks.title: The local mask likelihood omits permitted cross-block dependence
checks.claimContext: Equation (2) permits a feature’s observation probability \(\rho_j(h,Y)\) to depend on the entire latent vector. Equation (7) instead conditions its mask only on the feature’s own block latent. Conditional independence of the emissions does not establish that additional locality of the masks.

checks.contextAfter: For a hardware-efficient implementation of $\mathcal{P}\{\cdot\}$ , we represent $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ using a custom axis-reordered 2D RFFT format. Standard 2D RFFT formats scatter non-redundant frequency components across non-contiguous memory segments, necessitating costly copying or strided memory gathering. checks.claim:
All 89579 cached characters read through EOF: Sections 1-6, equations 1-8, references, Appendices A-C.6 and Tables 1-18.
DAG semantics, seven hierarchy metrics and aggregation, graph construction/pruning, activation binarization, encoder comparisons, ImageNet check, sibling redundancy and cophenetic adaptation.
checks.explanation:
No issue was found in the checked claims. There is no formal theorem claiming that unsupervised scores uniquely recover semantics. Reconstructed Eq.1 as ||sum_i w_i e_i/||e_i||||^2/(sum_i w_i)^2 when all pairs including diagonals are used. Hence its actual range is [0,1], contained in the declared [-1,1]; the looser range is not false. Min-max normalization of a constant feature is undefined, but dead/rare feature exclusion mitigates this; not established as an executed failure. Eq.2 is a binary proxy, Eq.3 averages exactly n(n-1)/2 sibling similarities. Equations 4–6 are distinct conditional sample frequencies, not equivalent logical requirements: high probability of a_p>=a_c need not imply E[a_p]>=E[a_c]. The paper calls these metrics/proxies and allows per-sample exceptions, so this distinction does not falsify a theorem. Spearman on max-child activations is a declared monotonic association measure, not a causal proof that children suppress parents. Equal TopK is explicitly a comparison convention. Weighted CCA in B.4 and unweighted implication need not match exactly; separate held-out graph/evaluation splits also explain deviations below .9. H-SAE 361 experts times 16 children gives 5776 edges and 6137 nodes; nonnested widths sum to 6144. review-neurips-2026-153186.title: Covariate-Adjusted Deep Causal Learning for Heterogeneous Panel Data Models

checks.location: Section 2.3, Theorem 2.1 (cached text line 388) and preceding Assumptions 1–3
checks.claim: Assumptions 1–3 plus the stated dimensional and size conditions yield vanishing treated-post counterfactual MSE under suitable DNN parameters.
checks.explanation: The printed conditions allow post-treatment factors to take values never seen before treatment. Two smooth treated-unit loading functions can agree at every pre-treatment value and differ afterwards; a constant change in treatment effect then makes the observed panels identical. Even revealing the factors does not identify the untreated treated-post means. The resulting risk lower bound contradicts the vanishing rate under the printed fixed-dimension and sample-size conditions.
checks.demonstration:
Let $m\to\infty$ and choose
$$
\begin{aligned}
K=K_1=P=B&=1, &\beta&=3/2,\\
N_1=N_2=n&=m, &T_1=T_2&=m^2.
\end{aligned}
$$
Let the covariates be independent uniform variables on $[0,1]$, set $g_t=0$, and take independent centered Gaussian errors of fixed positive variance. Independently, draw symmetric factors from $\{-1/3,1/3\}$ before treatment and $\{-1,1\}$ afterwards. These choices satisfy Assumptions 1–2 with constants independent of $m$.

In both worlds use control loadings $\phi_i(x)=x$ and control treatment effects zero. For treated units take
$$
\begin{aligned}
\phi^{(0)}(x)&=x/5,\\
\phi^{(1)}(x)&=x/5+(9x^2-1)/24,\\
\tau^{(0)}&=3/5,\qquad \tau^{(1)}=4/15.
\end{aligned}
$$
Define potential outcomes by $Y_{it}^{(j)}(w)=\phi_i^{(j)}(F_t)+\tau_i^{(j)}w+\varepsilon_{it}$. They have static treatment effects and no interference. The two treated loadings agree at the pre-treatment support and differ by $1/3$ at the post-treatment support. The treatment-effect difference is $-1/3$, so coupling the factors, covariates and errors makes every observed outcome identical. The untreated treated-post conditional means nevertheless differ by $1/3$. Revealing the entire factor sequence would not distinguish the worlds.

For Assumption 3, give the $m$ control coordinates weight $1/m$ and the treated coordinates weight zero, and use $\rho(z)=z$. Then $\rho(M\phi(x))=x$ for every $x\in[-1,1]$, with largest entry $1/m$ and exactly $m$ nonzeros. This is an exact inverse of the noiseless control-loading map; it is not a claim of exact finite-sample recovery through Gaussian noise. The identity decoder and zero covariate functions satisfy the specified $\beta=3/2$ smoothness. Both treated loadings are also smooth and bounded on the factor domain.

Any estimator and coupled internal randomness give the same estimate in both worlds. If $a$ is its error relative to world zero in one target cell, then
$$
\frac{a^2+(a-1/3)^2}{2}
=(a-1/6)^2+\frac1{36}.
$$
For the average squared target-block errors $Q_0,Q_1$, this gives $(Q_0+Q_1)/2\ge1/36$ on every coupled realization. Taking expectations proves the lower bound for the risk printed in the theorem. It also rules out convergence of both block errors to zero in probability: the union of the events $Q_0\ge1/36$ and $Q_1\ge1/36$ has probability one, so at least one event has probability at least $1/2$ at each $m$.

All printed size conditions hold: $K_1\ge K$, $\log(2m+2m^2)=o(m)$, $N_1=N_2$ and $T_1=T_2$. For every fixed positive dimension $k$, the asserted rate becomes
$$
O\!\left(m^{-1}\log^4m+m^{-3/(3+k)}\log^5m\right)=o(1).
$$
In particular, $k=P=K=K_1=1$ gives the stated $m^{-3/4}$ term. The source leaves lowercase $k$ undefined, but this does not permit consistency for any fixed-dimension interpretation. Both identical-data worlds cannot satisfy the conclusion.

u_{m post}/d
u_{m pre}\le C_0<\infty$. A time-invariant factor law has $C_0=1$. Either condition excludes this counterexample, but neither alone proves the original estimator's rate.

The following conditional risk-transfer lemma states what overlap supplies. Work in a common factor coordinate system, with factors estimable from controls and fitted loadings that are uniformly $L_0$-Lipschitz. Let $a_{N,T}$ bound their average population squared loading error under $
u_{m pre}$, let $b_{N,T}$ bound post-treatment factor-estimation error, and let $c_{N,T}$ bound post-treatment covariate-effect error. These are component risk assumptions, not conclusions proved here for CoDEAL. Use evaluation draws independent of the fitted functions, or require domination conditional on the training data; empirical training loss alone cannot replace $a_{N,T}$.

checks.demonstration: For balanced contexts and uniform queries, Lemma D.8 gives \(L_k=\tfrac12(1-A_k)^2\). At \(T_1\), the two cross logits are equal, while \(\alpha_k=\gamma_k^2\alpha_*\). Take \(\epsilon=0.01\), \(\alpha_*=\log3\), \(\gamma_1=0.8\), \(\gamma_2=0.2\). These shifts are realized by \(v_1=e_1,v_2=e_2\), \(u_1=0.8e_1+0.6e_3\), and \(u_2=0.2e_2+\sqrt{0.96}e_4\), satisfying the stated orthogonality conditions. The common cross logit is \(-0.16\log3\), and the two attention probabilities are approximately \(0.70659\) and \(0.55471\). Thus the losses are \(0.04304<0.09914\), the reverse of the lemma. For the separate step inference, \(\alpha_{\max}=2\), \(\eta=1/2\) meets the printed cap but gives \(1-e^2/2<0\).
checks.repair: Reverse the inequality and prove the ordering using the attention margins, rather than only the self logits. In the paper's balanced-context, uniform-query population model, set \(m_k=\alpha_k-\beta_{\mathrm{other},k}\) and \(A_k=\sigma(m_k)\). Differentiating the stated loss under population GD gives \[m_k^+=m_k+2\eta\sigma(m_k)(1-\sigma(m_k))^2.\] Let \(H(m)=2\sigma(m)(1-\sigma(m))^2\). Since \(|H'(m)|\le1/2\), the update map has derivative at least \(1/2\) for \(0\le\eta\le1\). With \(m_1(T_1)>m_2(T_1)\), it preserves strict margin order at every finite step, and hence preserves \(L_1<L_2\). This is a sufficient replacement step condition; downstream statements must use that condition and the reversed ordering. It does not certify their separate stopping-time or forgetting bounds.

Use two prompts \(u,v\) and two concepts. Pre-edit activations are \(0,1/2\); post-edit activations are \(-1,1/2\). The two concept-presence probability vectors are respectively \((1,0),(0,1)\) before editing and \((0,0),(0,1)\) afterward. The edited image for \(u\) contains neither concept. Every cross-model, cross-prompt pair satisfies the probability Lipschitz assumption with \(L=2\).

The target is erased for both prompts, so \(\varepsilon=0\). Its activation moves by one, satisfying \(\Delta=1/2\). With \(\rho=1\), the fattened target and neighbor intervals are \([-1,1]\) and \([-1/2,3/2]\). Their overlap gives \(\kappa=3/4\). All non-target prompt mass lies at \(1/2\), inside that overlap, so even the explicit mass-volume requirement holds.

If \(\widehat p\) is the fraction falling in that neighbor union, its population value \(p_{\mathcal N}\) is a volume ratio and satisfies \(p_{\mathcal N}\le\kappa\).

Hoeffding’s inequality then gives, with probability at least \(1-\delta\),
\[\max\!\left\{0,\widehat p-\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{2m}}\right\}\le p_{\mathcal N}\le\kappa.\]
This requires a different sampling design and uncertainty calculation. The 50 selected prompt templates do not supply those premises.

review-neurips-2026-156750.title: RPP: A Certified Poisoned-Sample Detection Framework for Backdoor Attacks under Dataset Imbalance

checks.location: Theorem 5.1 Eq.(6), Appendix A.1 Eqs.(20)-(23); work/text/156750.txt:242-266,2022-2059
checks.claim: The trigger-norm lower inequality is sufficient for poisoned-sample detection.
checks.explanation: The derivation constrains the trigger norm when a score upper bound is already true. It does not imply that the score is below the calibration threshold. The implication cannot be reversed by substituting that threshold for the unknown score bound.
checks.demonstration:
Use a binary classifier on \((u,v)\) with
\[p_1(u,v)=0.1+0.8e^{-(u-3)^2/2},\qquad p_0=1-p_1,\qquad\sigma=1.\]
Take clean source \((0,0)\) and trigger \((3,0)\). At the poisoned point, the target probability is \(0.9\) and strictly decreases after Gaussian noise almost surely, satisfying the probability-decrease assumption. The clean noisy target probability is \(\bar p_t=0.1+0.8e^{-9/4}/\sqrt2\approx0.15962281\), and the poisoned RPP is
\[s_p=0.8(1-1/\sqrt2)\approx0.23431458.\]
Choose the valid upper bound \(\zeta=s_p\). The stated trigger lower bound is approximately \(1.42403951\), below the actual norm three.

Calibrate on 100 independent samples from the balanced clean distribution on \((0,0)\), label zero, and \((3,10)\), label one. Both labels match the classifier’s argmax, and the poisoned input is distinct from both clean inputs. The clean scores are \(s_0\approx0.05760190\) and \(s_p\). For \(\alpha=0.05\), the threshold is the sixth-smallest score. With probability
\[1-2^{-100}\sum_{j=0}^{5}\binom{100}{j}=1-6.2616\times10^{-23},\]
it equals \(s_0<s_p\), so the poisoned point is missed despite satisfying the norm condition.
checks.repair:
Keep the direction of the proved implication. If \(L(a)\le s_p\le\zeta\), where \(L(a)=p-\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\bar p_t)+a)\) and \(a=\|\delta\|_2/\sigma\), then \(L(a)\le\zeta\) yields the stated necessary lower bound on \(a\).

A sufficient detection certificate instead needs a valid score upper bound \(s_p\le U_p\) and the separate condition \(U_p\le\widehat q\). These imply detection directly for the inclusive rule. Estimating or bounding \(U_p\) requires its own assumptions and uncertainty control; the trigger lower bound supplies neither.
checks.scope: This refutes the theorem’s sufficient-detection claim for population RPP under its stated assumptions. It does not dispute the Gaussian transfer inequality or evaluate finite-noise certification code.
checks.title: The trigger-norm inequality is necessary, not sufficient for detection
checks.claimContext: Theorem 5.1 combines a Gaussian probability-transfer bound with an assumed upper bound on poisoned-sample RPP, then presents the resulting trigger-norm inequality as sufficient for detecting the poisoned sample below a calibrated score threshold.
checks.whyItMatters: A certificate must imply the detector’s threshold decision, rather than merely be compatible with an assumed favorable score.
checks.checkedLocation: Theorem 5.1, Equation (6); Appendix A.1, Equations (20)–(23)

checks.location: Corollary 5.2 Eq.(7), Appendix A.2 Eq.(24); work/text/156750.txt:272-278,2083-2091
checks.claim: All triggers satisfying Theorem5.1 assumptions obey the displayed upper norm bound.
checks.explanation: The probability-decrease assumption bounds the actual noisy probability below the peak probability. An upper bound on that noisy probability can still exceed the peak. Positivity of the gap to that upper envelope is an extra condition, not a consequence of the assumption.
checks.demonstration:
Take the smooth binary classifier \(p_1(u,v)=0.1+0.8e^{-(u-3)^2/2}\), clean input \((0,0)\), unit Gaussian noise and trigger \((3,0)\). Its poisoned target probability is \(p=0.9\), while \(\bar p_t\approx0.15962281\). The corollary gives an upper norm of approximately \(2.27756090\), but the trigger norm is three.

The actual smoothed poisoned probability is approximately \(0.66568542<0.9\), as required. The Gaussian upper envelope is instead
\[\Phi\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\bar p_t)+3\bigr)\approx0.97746447>0.9.\]
Both facts can hold at once: a valid upper bound need not be attained or lie below the peak.
checks.repair:
Retain the valid lower score bound
\[s_p\ge\max\!\left\{0,p-\Phi\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\bar p_t)+\|\delta\|_2/\sigma\bigr)\right\}.\]
The maximum with zero follows because RPP is nonnegative. Remove the universal upper trigger bound. If positivity of the expression inside the maximum is separately assumed, monotonicity of \(\Phi\) yields the strict upper-norm condition, but that new premise is equivalent to the condition being imposed and is not supplied by probability decrease.
checks.scope: This refutes Corollary 5.2’s universal upper trigger bound. The Gaussian comparison itself remains valid.
checks.title: A probability upper envelope does not impose an upper bound on trigger size
checks.claimContext: Corollary 5.2 claims an upper trigger-norm bound under Theorem 5.1’s assumptions. Appendix A.2 treats the gap between the unperturbed target probability and a Gaussian upper envelope as positive.
checks.whyItMatters: The paper’s proposed certified trigger interval cannot use an upper endpoint that excludes triggers satisfying its own assumptions.
checks.checkedLocation: Corollary 5.2, Equation (7); Appendix A.2, Equation (24)

checks.location: Theorem 5.3 Eq.(9), Appendix A.3 rank argument; work/text/156750.txt:287-299,2093-2106
checks.claim: The lower empirical quantile gives the stated benign-above-threshold coverage.
checks.explanation: The test rank is uniform among \(n+1\) observations for continuous iid scores. The calibration threshold leaves \(k\) test ranks below it, not the number used in the stated correction.
checks.demonstration:
Under continuous iid scores,
\[\Pr(S_{\mathrm{test}}\le S_{(k)})=\frac{k}{n+1},\qquad\Pr(S_{\mathrm{test}}\ge S_{(k)})=\frac{n+1-k}{n+1}.\]
For \(n=100\), \(\alpha=0.05\), and \(k=6\), the actual second probability is \(95/101\approx0.940594\); the claimed lower bound is approximately \(0.959901\).

These scores are realizable as RPP: take the binary threshold classifier \(p_1(z)=\mathbf1\{z\ge0\}\), unit Gaussian noise, and benign inputs \(X=-\Phi^{-1}(U)\), where \(U\) is uniform on \((0.1,0.2)\). Every input is positive and its RPP is exactly \(\Phi(-X)=U\).
checks.repair:
Replace the lower bound by
\[\Pr(S_{\mathrm{test}}\ge S_{(k)})\ge1-\frac{k}{n+1},\qquad k=\lceil\alpha(n+1)\rceil.\]
It is an equality for continuous iid scores. For arbitrary ties, break tied ranks randomly only for the proof: the event \(S_{\mathrm{test}}<S_{(k)}\) implies randomized rank at most \(k\), so the same lower bound holds. If \(k=n+1\), define the threshold as \(+\infty\), giving the trivial zero lower bound. This corrects the formula without changing the detector.
checks.scope: This is a local order-statistic and rounding correction of size \(O(1/n)\). It is separate from the stronger conditional guarantee and tie-handling failures in Theorem 5.4.
checks.title: The lower-quantile coverage formula has the wrong rank correction
checks.claimContext: Theorem 5.3 uses the calibration order statistic \(q=S_{(k)}\), where \(k=\lceil\alpha(n+1)\rceil\), and claims the following lower bound for a clean test score. For the calculation below, \(1\le k\le n\).
checks.whyItMatters: The rank calculation determines the finite-sample coverage actually provided by the printed quantile.
checks.checkedLocation: Theorem 5.3, Equations (8)–(9); Appendix A.3

checks.location: Theorem 5.4 Eq.(10), Appendix A.4 conditional rank equality; work/text/156750.txt:304-312,2108-2121
checks.claim: The FPR conditional on every realized calibration set is deterministically bounded by alpha+1/(n+1).
checks.explanation: Once calibration is fixed, the threshold is fixed and the test false-positive probability is its population CDF value. This value varies across calibration samples; uniform marginal rank does not make it deterministically bounded by its mean.
checks.demonstration:
For a continuous score CDF \(F\) and \(q=S_{(k)}\), the conditional false-positive probability is \(F(q)\). The probability integral transform gives
\[F(S_{(k)})\sim\operatorname{Beta}(k,n+1-k),\]
which has positive probability above any number below one.

Concretely, use the uniform RPP construction on \((0.1,0.2)\) from the order-statistic example, with \(n=100\), \(\alpha=0.05\), and \(k=6\). With positive probability \(0.8^{100}\), every calibration score exceeds \(0.12\). Then \(q>0.12\) and the conditional false-positive probability exceeds \(0.2\), whereas the asserted bound is approximately \(0.059901\).
checks.repair:
For continuous iid scores, the correct marginal statement is
\[\mathbb E_{\mathcal S}F(S_{(k)})=\Pr(S_{\mathrm{test}}\le S_{(k)})=\frac{k}{n+1}\le\alpha+\frac1{n+1}.\]
A conditional-probability bound must itself carry confidence over calibration. For example, if \(B_{a,b}^{-1}\) denotes a beta quantile, then
\[\Pr_{\mathcal S}\!\left\{F(S_{(k)})\le B_{k,n+1-k}^{-1}(1-\delta)\right\}=1-\delta.\]
The beta order-statistic law proves this statement. It does not give the displayed deterministic guarantee for every calibration set.
checks.scope: This failure occurs without ties. The separate inclusive-tie issue remains relevant when continuity is not assumed. Appendix A.4 already describes the beta variation across calibration sets. That distribution supplies the high-probability repair; its mean does not give a deterministic guarantee for each calibration set.
checks.title: Marginal rank calibration does not give a bound for every realized calibration set
checks.claimContext: Theorem 5.4 conditions on the entire calibration score set \(\mathcal S\), yet bounds the resulting false-positive probability by a deterministic rank fraction. Its proof uses the unconditional rank symmetry of an iid test score and calibration scores. Here \(k=\lceil\alpha(n+1)\rceil\), with \(1\le k\le n\).
checks.whyItMatters: An average false-positive guarantee and a guarantee conditional on the chosen calibration set answer different operational questions.
checks.verificationNote: Appendix A.4 subsequently invokes a beta distribution and its variance over calibration samples. That argument recognizes the variability; it does not justify the preceding deterministic conditional inequality.
checks.checkedLocation: Theorem 5.4, Equation (10); Appendix A.4, conditional rank argument

checks.location: Theorem 5.4 Eq.(10) and asymptotic assertion, Algorithm1 threshold rule; work/text/156750.txt:304-312,2945-2975
checks.claim: The lower-quantile <= detector has finite-sample and asymptotic FPR control for arbitrary iid benign score distributions.
checks.explanation: An atom at the threshold can contain much more probability mass than the intended lower tail. The inclusive comparison flags that entire atom, so even a marginal rank bound and the asymptotic claim can fail.
checks.demonstration:
Take a constant binary probability classifier \(p(z)=(0.9,0.1)\), any positive Gaussian noise level, and iid benign inputs all labeled with its first class. The classifier is correct on every benign input. Its RPP is identically zero, both as a population expectation and with any finite number of noise samples.

Every calibration threshold is therefore zero, and the inclusive rule flags every clean test point: \(Z_n=1\) for all \(n\). With \(\alpha=0.05\), \(\xi=0.01\),
\[\Pr(Z_n\le\alpha+\xi)=0\quad\text{for every }n,\]
contrary to the claimed limit of one. The trigger-specific probability-decrease assumption is not a premise of these clean-score calibration theorems.
checks.repair:
Set \(k=\lceil\alpha(n+1)\rceil\), with threshold \(+\infty\) if \(k=n+1\). Use strict rejection, \(S_{\mathrm{test}}<S_{(k)}\), or specify a valid randomized conformal rank rule. For the strict rule, exchangeability with randomized tie ranks used only in the proof gives
\[\Pr(S_{\mathrm{test}}<S_{(k)})\le\frac{k}{n+1}\le\alpha+\frac1{n+1}.\]
This marginal bound holds for arbitrary score distributions and rejects none of the constant-score example.

The asymptotic conditional statement also follows for this strict rule under iid calibration: if \(F_n\) is the empirical CDF, then
\[F(S_{(k)}-)\le\frac{k-1}{n}+\sup_s|F_n(s)-F(s)|.\]
Uniform convergence of the empirical CDF makes the second term vanish, while \((k-1)/n\to\alpha\). Thus the conditional false-positive probability is at most \(\alpha+\xi\) with probability tending to one. The deterministic finite-sample conditional bound still does not follow.
checks.scope: This refutes both the inclusive detector’s distribution-free marginal control and its stated asymptotic claim. It concerns the printed mathematical rule, including its finite-noise constant-score case, not benchmark arithmetic.
checks.title: Inclusive thresholding can flag every clean sample when scores tie
checks.claimContext: Algorithm 1 flags scores at or below the calibrated lower quantile. Theorem 5.4 gives finite-sample and asymptotic false-positive control without a no-ties assumption or a randomized tie rule.
checks.whyItMatters: Tie handling is part of the detector specification and can change its false-positive rate from the nominal level to one.
checks.checkedLocation: Theorem 5.4 and its asymptotic statement; Algorithm 1, inclusive threshold rule
